name: Skirrid–Arthur's Stone Castles Ley
who: G. H. Piper (Woolhope Club, 1882), cited by Alfred Watkins (1922)
desc: A line drawn north from the Skirrid mountain to Arthur's Stone, said to pass a run of hill points and Norman castles along the Monnow and Golden Valley. Watkins quoted it as early independent evidence for his leys.

name: Croft Ambrey–Y Fan Dringarth Ley
desc: One of Watkins' long cross-border leys, running from the Croft Ambrey hillfort south-west through churches and mounds in the Wye valley to Slwch camp at Brecon and a Brecon Beacons peak.

name: Bailey Hill–May Hill Ley
desc: A Watkins ley from Bailey Hill above Knighton to May Hill near Longhope, said to cross Presteigne, Holmer, Fownhope church, Capler Camp and Linton church on the way.

name: Four Stones–Breinton Ley
desc: Watkins read the Four Stones near New Radnor as sighting posts. He traced this ley from Bach Hill in Radnor Forest through the stones and Walton, then on through Kenchester church to Breinton church across the Wye.

name: Little Mountain–Malvern Priory Ley
desc: Starting at Little Mountain near Westbrook, this ley is said to run through Arthur's Stone and a string of Herefordshire churches to St Ann's Well and the Priory at Great Malvern.

name: Long Meg–Mayburgh–Cockpit Line
who: 'Blackledge', Megalithic Portal forum (2026), tested in the Portal's Ley Finder
desc: A roughly 17 km straight line through the centres of Long Meg and Her Daughters, Mayburgh Henge and the Cockpit circle, raising the idea of coordinated monument building. Extended, it passes close to the Kirk Stone at Kirkstone Pass.

name: Devil's Arrows–Thornborough Ley
who: Norrie Ward (1969); Devereux & Thomson (1979); Pennick & Devereux (1989)
desc: The axis of the Thornborough henges, extended south-east through Nunwick henge, points to the Devil's Arrows standing stones at Boroughbridge about 17.7 km away. Ley hunters and some archaeologists have long cited it.

name: Rudston D Cursus–Monolith
who: Paul Bennett, The Northern Antiquarian (2013), after I. M. Stead (1976)
desc: The Rudston D cursus runs south from Burton Fleming parallel to the Gypsey Race and heads straight for the Rudston monolith, ending just short of the churchyard stone.

name: Rudston B Cursus–Monolith
who: Hedges & Buckley (1981); confirmed by Paul Devereux (1989)
desc: Rudston B cursus runs north-east from near Kilham Grange. Projected eastwards, its line is said to hit the Rudston monolith, one of several cursuses that seem to focus on the stone.

name: Almscliffe Solstice Line
desc: A natural solstice line between Little Almscliffe and Almscliffe Crag: winter sunrise seen from the smaller crag, summer sunset from the greater. The lost Staniston Hill standing stone is said to sit near its midpoint.

name: Kilmartin Cairns–Dun Chonallaich
desc: The Bronze Age linear cemetery of five cairns along Kilmartin Glen runs roughly north–south. Bennett argues its line was deliberately aimed at the hill of Dun Chonallaich about three miles to the north.

name: Brodgar–Watchstone–Barnhouse Line
desc: Spence proposed that the centre of the Ring of Brodgar, the Watchstone and the Barnhouse Stone form one line marking calendar sunrises and sunsets. Lockyer kept the line but tied it to Beltane sunset and Hallowmas sunrise.

name: Maeshowe–Barnhouse Stone Line
desc: Maeshowe's entrance passage lines up with the Barnhouse Stone about 750 m south-west. Looking out, the line marks sunset about ten days before the winter solstice; looking the other way, midsummer sunrise.

name: Stenness–Watchstone–Brodgar Avenue
desc: Early antiquarians proposed a stone-lined avenue joining the Stones of Stenness to the Ring of Brodgar, with the Watchstone as its last surviving stone. Geophysics has since found no trace of such a route.

name: Callanish Lunar Standstill
who: Popular theory; observations by Margaret Curtis and Gerald Ponting
desc: At the major lunar standstill, the moon is said to skim the 'Sleeping Beauty' hills, set towards Glen Langadale in Harris, then briefly reappear among the Callanish stones. Some read this as a deliberate ceremonial design.

name: Lundin Links Lunar Line
who: Alexander Thom (1971); disputed by Douglas Heggie (1981)
desc: Thom argued that the tall Lundin stones mark the minor-standstill moon setting on Cormie Hill, while the same moon rises grazing the Bass Rock across the Forth.

name: Gleneagles–Boat Stone–White Stone
who: Andrew Finlayson, The Stones of Strathearn (2010)
desc: A south-westerly alignment of Strathearn standing stones, from the Gleneagles pair through the fallen Boat Stone to the White Stone near Dunblane. It holds on a 1:50,000 map but misses by 20–30 yards at larger scales.

name: Twmbarlwm Pleiades Line
desc: Sivertsen proposed a line from the Twmbarlwm cairns to the western cairn on Gray Hill, continuing to a short solar stone row, which he dated to about 2500 BC via the rising Pleiades.

name: Twmbarlwm–Druidstone–Flat Holm
desc: A line from the northernmost Twmbarlwm cairn, past its other two cairns, south to the middle of Flat Holm. On the way it meets the Druidstone standing stone at St Mellons, which Sivertsen said 'begs the question of intention'.

name: Parc-y-Meirw–Mount Leinster
desc: Thom suggested the Parc-y-Meirw stone row in Pembrokeshire points WNW to a minor northern moonset over Mount Leinster in Ireland, about 91 miles across the Irish Sea. Burl doubted it.

name: Boscawen-Un–Perranuthnoe Ley
who: John Michell, The Ley Hunter (1970), from a Lockyer bearing
desc: Michell's line A1 runs from the Boscawen-Un circle through a stone cross and the Tresvennack pillar, and may extend to St Piran's church at Perranuthnoe.

name: Tregeseal–Lanyon–Chysauster Ley
desc: Michell's line B1(c) links the Tregeseal circle with Lanyon Quoit, a standing stone, and the Chysauster courtyard-house village, one of several West Penwith alignments he plotted.

name: King Stone–Salford Cross Ley
who: Local ley tradition, recorded in The Northern Antiquarian (2010)
desc: A ley said to run from the King Stone through the Rollright circle and Little Rollright church, where a standing stone is set in the walling, to the Salford cross-base and a lost cross beyond.

name: Bincknoll–Beckhampton–Marden Ley
who: Devereux & Thomson, The Ley Hunter's Companion (1979)
desc: A roughly 13-mile north–south ley across the Avebury landscape, from Bincknoll Castle through the Beckhampton Penning earthwork to Marden Henge in the Vale of Pewsey.

name: Wilmington Ley
who: Devereux & Thomson, The Ley Hunter's Companion (1979)
desc: A short Sussex ley from Wilmington church past the priory to the Long Man hill figure and the barrow on Windover Hill, ending in Friston Forest.
